title: Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu
hookLine: Nanak's mother loved him gently; his father, an accountant, worried for his future

lines: A NEW PART: THE PEOPLE AROUND THE GURUS.
cards: A father counts coins into his son's hand. Go to the market, he says. Buy well, sell well, come home with a profit.
The son comes home with empty hands and no goods. On the road, he says, he met holy men who hadn't eaten, and he fed them. That was the true bargain.
The father is furious. The mother, as tradition remembers her, is gentler. A new part of the path begins today: the people around the Gurus, starting at home, with Mata Tripta and Mehta Kalu.

teach.h: THE TRUE BARGAIN: A JANAMSAKHI STORY.
teach.b: The story of the coins isn't in the Granth. It comes from the janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs remember it as the sacha sauda, the true bargain.
The janamsakhis sketch his parents in a few strokes.
His father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts: a practical man with a practical hope, that his son would find steady work and get on in the world.
His mother, Mata Tripta, the stories remember as gentle, the one who loved the boy as he was. The stories don't make Mehta Kalu a villain. A father worried about money and a future isn't a bad man.
He's a father. In one story the boy grows quiet and withdrawn, lying for days without wanting to eat, and the worried family calls in a physician. Here the Granth itself has a line.

teach.h: A PHYSICIAN WHO MISSED THE ACHE.
teach.b: In a salok in Raag Malar, on Ang 1279, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: they called the physician to treat me; he took my arm and felt for the illness; the simple physician doesn't know the pain is deep inside, in the heart.
Whether that salok was spoken in that very room, the sources don't settle. But it fits.
The family's worry was real, and so was their love. They just couldn't see where the ache was. Neither parent fully understood their son, and both of them loved him.
Love and worry live in the same house, often in the same parent.

how: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Nanak's childhood from the janamsakhis, especially at Gurpurab, and the sacha sauda, the true bargain, is among the stories children hear at home and in gurdwara classes.

o: a nurse who raises a child

games.q: the house at the start — tap the pairs.
p: didn't know the pain was in the heart

s: the story of the true bargain is told in the Guru Granth Sahib
it comes from the janamsakhis, the old life-stories of Guru Nanak.
the stories make Mehta Kalu a villain
he's a practical father worried about his son's future.

games.q: you're Nanak, on the road with your father's coins, and you meet holy men who haven't eaten. what do you do?
o: buy goods and sell them for a profit, as asked.
feed them, and call that the true bargain.
split the money and do a little of both.
games.why: in the janamsakhi, he feeds them and comes home empty-handed; Sikhs remember it as the sacha sauda.

practice: Bring to mind someone who worried about you, a parent, a grandparent, a guardian, an older friend, and one thing they worried over, maybe something that annoyed you at the time.
Look underneath it for the love that was holding it; you don't have to agree with the worry, just see what it was made of. If you pray, let Waheguru come with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Mata. A title of honor for the Gurus' mothers and wives: Guru Nanak's mother, gentle, her husband worried, and love and worry living in the same home.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mata, mother; a title of honor for the Gurus' mothers and wives.

carryVoice: Your line: love and worry. One house, often one parent, holds them both. See you tomorrow.
